Outgassing and seal library

Typical values from the book (figures 10.1–10.3, tables 10.1–10.2, appendix D). Real rates depend on cleaning, history and pumping time; measure for critical systems.

Screening other materials? NASA's outgassing database lists TML and CVCM (ASTM E595: 24 h at 125 °C in vacuum) for thousands of polymers, adhesives and cables. A common acceptance limit is TML ≤ 1 % and CVCM ≤ 0.1 %. These are mass-loss percentages, not outgassing rates, so use them to choose materials and take the rates for the calculator from the table above or from measurements.

Gas library
Method, assumptions & sources
  • Source. Formulas and data from Vacuum Science and Technology (Suurmeijer, Mulder, Verhoeven): kinetic gas theory (ch. 1), gas flow and conductance (ch. 3), pumps and pumping systems (ch. 4), seals (ch. 9), materials, outgassing and permeation (ch. 10, appendix D). The calculator reproduces the worked example of §3.17 and exercises 3-1, 3-2, 3-3, 4-5, 4-6, 4-8 and 4-17 (see the tests in the repository).
  • Conductance. Molecular flow: orifice (3.97), short tubes with the Clausing factor 4d/(4d + 3l) (3.109–3.110), long tubes (3.107), rectangular ducts (3.112–3.114), annular gaps (3.105, 3.116) and bends as extra length α·d (3.118). Viscous flow: Poiseuille (3.89, 3.91, 3.93). Transition: the empirical f(d·p) of (3.123) written in d/λ so it applies to every gas; orifices are interpolated between molecular and choked flow (assumption). Conductances scale with √(T/M) (3.120).
  • Gas loads. Metals: q = q₁ₕ·(1 h/t) with 10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁵ or 10⁻⁴ Pa·m³/(s·m²) at 1 h (figure 10.1, table 10.1); polymers and ceramics per figure 10.2 (≈1/t^0.6–0.85); after bakeout the values of appendix D. Permeation through O-rings Q = P(T)·Δp·F·πD with the Arrhenius fit of figure 10.3 and a seal geometry factor F = 2, which reproduces the Viton example of §4.11.1 and exercise 4-8. A double O-ring with pumped interspace sees only the interspace pressure (§9.2.1).
  • Pump-down. V·dp/dt = Q(t) − S_eff·(p − p_u), integrated with exponential steps (7.4, 7.7); pump speed falls as S₀·(1 − p_u/p) (7.8), the throughput is limited by choked flow through the narrowest section of the line, an optional Roots pump takes over below its switch-on pressure, and the high-vacuum pump at the crossover pressure. The 1/t outgassing law is extrapolated beyond its tens of hours of validity with a warning.
  • Pumps. Ultimate pressures, working ranges and typical speeds from the tables of chapter 4; the working range ends 5 to 10 times above the ultimate pressure. Backing pump: S_b ≥ Q_max/p_b,max (exercises 4-3, 4-6).
  • Wall strength (not in the book). Cylinders: Windenburg–Trilling elastic buckling with the long-cylinder limit 2E/(1−ν²)·(t/D)³; spheres: 0.25·E·(t/Rₒ)², a lower bound that, with the default safety factor 4, equals the elastic allowable pressure of ASME VIII-1 UG-28(d); flat plates under 1 atm: Roark's formulas for clamped or simply supported rectangular and circular plates. Ports, flanges, welds and stiffeners need a separate check to the applicable pressure-vessel code.
  • Not included. Gas mixtures and partial pressures, pump speed curves from data sheets, compression ratio of turbo pumps, desorption peaks during bakeout, diffusion-limited outgassing, virtual leaks, conductance of complex geometries (use a fixed conductance element), thermal transpiration.
  • Verification against other sources. Besides the book examples, the tests compare the calculator with standard handbook values for air at 20 °C (orifice 11.6 L/s per cm², long tube 12.1·d³/l, Poiseuille 135·d⁴·p̄/l, choked orifice ≈ 20 L/s per cm²; d and l in cm, p̄ in mbar): all agree within 1 %. Cylinder buckling agrees within 5 % with the von Mises formula of EN 13445-3. Known deviation: the book's short-tube factor 4d/(4d + 3l) is up to about 11 % higher than the exact Clausing values, so short-tube conductances are slightly optimistic.

Vacuum Chamber Calculator

Version 1.1 · by Eren Tozlu

A free, browser-based tool for designing a vacuum chamber and its pumping system. It adds up the gas load from outgassing, permeation through seals and leaks, calculates the conductance of the pumping lines and the effective pumping speed, simulates the pump-down from atmosphere and checks the walls against collapse. All calculations run in your browser.

The formulas, material data and worked examples come from the textbook Vacuum Science and Technology by Bart Suurmeijer, Theo Mulder and Jan Verhoeven; equation numbers in the step-by-step calculation refer to it. The wall check uses Roark's plate formulas and the Windenburg–Trilling buckling formula. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the authors or publisher.

Made by Eren Tozlu. More engineering tools and projects at ehcrea.com.

Open source under the MIT License; the source code is on GitHub.

Disclaimer. Results are engineering estimates for concept design, not a certified calculation. The calculations reproduce the book's worked examples and were cross-checked against standard handbook values and the elastic buckling formula of EN 13445-3 (see the notes below the results). Known limits: the book's short-tube Clausing factor gives conductances up to about 11 % higher than exact values; outgassing and permeation data vary by an order of magnitude with material batch, cleaning and history; pump data are typical values, so use the manufacturer's curves for the actual pump. Verify critical systems by measurement and have pressure-bearing parts, ports and welds checked to the applicable code (e.g. ASME VIII-1 or EN 13445). The tool is provided as is, without any warranty; use it at your own risk.

How to use the Vacuum Chamber Calculator

New here? Pick an example from Load application example… in the toolbar, then change one value at a time and watch the pump-down curve.

Six steps

  1. Chamber: shape, inner dimensions, wall material and thicknesses.
  2. Pressure & gas: the base pressure you need, the pumping time at which it must be reached, the gas and the temperature.
  3. Gas loads: wall cleanliness and bakeout, internal parts with their surface area, the elastomer seals (O-rings) and the allowed leak rate. A process gas flow only counts in operation.
  4. Roughing pump and its line from the chamber, optionally with a Roots booster.
  5. High-vacuum pump with its speed, crossover and backing pressure, and the line (ports, valves, baffles) between chamber and pump.
  6. Strength: safety factors for the atmospheric load on the walls.

Key ideas

Gas load Q
Gas entering the chamber per second [Pa·m³/s]. Below about 10⁻² Pa it is dominated by outgassing (mostly water vapour), which falls roughly as 1/t.
Conductance C
How easily gas flows through a tube or orifice. In molecular flow it depends only on geometry and gas, not on pressure. Elements in series add as 1/C = Σ1/Cᵢ.
Effective speed
S_eff = S·C/(S + C): the speed that actually reaches the chamber. A pump much larger than the line conductance is wasted.
Base pressure
p = Q/S_eff + p_u: gas load divided by the effective speed, plus the ultimate pressure of the pump.
Flow regime
Knudsen number Kn = λ/d: viscous below 0.01, molecular above 1. Roughing is mostly viscous, high vacuum molecular.

Reading the results

  • The chip shows OK, Check or Problem; each message says what to change and cites the section of the book.
  • The pump-down curve shows roughing (orange) and high vacuum (blue), the crossover point, the target and the pumping time.
  • Pumping lines lists every element; the limiting element is highlighted. Pump selection marks the pump types that suit the target; click a row to use one.
  • Step-by-step calculation writes out all formulas with their equation numbers. Copy link saves the design in a link; PDF report creates a printable report.

Free reading for students

All sources below are free to read online (in English) and are listed roughly from introductory to advanced.

  • Leybold – Fundamentals of Vacuum Technology: an introduction from gas physics to pumps, gauges and leak detection; also available as a free e-book.
  • Pfeiffer Vacuum – The Vacuum Technology Book: basic calculations (pressure, gas flow, conductance, pump-down time), components, pumps and measurement.
  • E. Al-Dmour – Fundamentals of Vacuum Physics and Technology: CERN Accelerator School lecture (2020): kinetic gas theory, gas flow and the main gas sources in a compact form.
  • P. Chiggiato – Vacuum Technology for Ion Sources: CERN Accelerator School lecture (2014): flow regimes, conductances, pump selection and an electrical analogy for pump-down.
  • M. Seidel – Accelerator Vacuum: CERN Accelerator School lecture (2021): pressure profiles along long tubes – why many systems are limited by conductance.
  • P. Chiggiato – Outgassing Properties of Vacuum Materials for Particle Accelerators: CERN Accelerator School lecture (2020): why surfaces release gas, the role of water vapour and bakeout, material choice; background to the 1/t law.
  • NASA – Outgassing Data for Selecting Spacecraft Materials: free searchable database of thousands of materials (adhesives, elastomers, plastics, tapes, cables) tested to ASTM E595. It reports TML (total mass loss, %) and CVCM (collected volatile condensable material, %), screening values for material selection; they are not outgassing rates and cannot be entered in the calculator directly.
  • V. Baglin – Cryopumping and Vacuum Systems: CERN Accelerator School lecture (2020): capture and cryopumps, applied to a large real system (LHC).
  • NASA SP-8007 – Buckling of Thin-Walled Circular Cylinders (2020): NASA design guideline on shell buckling and knock-down factors; background to the wall-strength check.
  • Short definitions on Wikipedia: Vacuum, Mean free path, Knudsen number, Free molecular flow, Outgassing, Vacuum pump, Ultra-high vacuum.
